stories.unplaced: A diplomatic proposal relayed through Qatar; no event site.
stories.title: Iran says its seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz, sent via Qatar, is 'still on the table'
stories.summary: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct 17 that Tehran had sent Washington, through mediator Qatar, a 'specific seven-day plan' under which the Strait of Hormuz could reopen and normal traffic resume if Iran's conditions were met: 'The choice is now America's.' On Oct 18 he told Iranian media the offer stood; if Washington accepts, the strait would open within six days and US-Iran talks would resume on the seventh. He said US military action had blocked the June memorandum of understanding. Iran first presented the plan in mid-September after a temporary ceasefire collapsed, and has acknowledged a US reply ('observations' it is reviewing); AP, via CBS, reported that Trump rejected a Tehran proposal to end the war and open the strait late last month. Iran has not published the full text, but Reuters reported its conditions include lifting the US blockade of its ports, cancelling US sanctions on its oil exports and a halt to hostilities on all fronts; Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary said Washington had not answered all seven conditions. A main sticking point is sequencing: Washington wants Iran's nuclear programme addressed from the start, while Tehran wants a first phase limited to reopening the strait. Trump told Newsmax on Oct 15 he would not use nuclear weapons or send ground troops and expects a deal after the Nov 3 midterms; CBS reported the Pentagon has prepared plans to use the MOAB on Iranian military sites if ordered.

analysis.text: Re-pitching a month-old offer before the midterms gives Trump a way to cut pump prices, while mines and attacks keep raising the cost of saying no. But Iran's published terms, an end to the port blockade and oil sanctions, are what Washington has shown no sign of giving up before Nov 3, and the US insistence on nuclear talks first makes a quick deal unlikely.

causes.why: The offer is the latest move in deadlocked indirect US-Iran talks
Mine strikes raise the price of rejecting Iran's terms

stories.unplaced: The IRGC gave no position for either tanker, and the other attacks were reported only as offshore areas.
stories.title: IRGC says a second tanker hit a mine; US says ships are being hit by projectiles as UKMTO logs a record week of attacks
stories.summary: Iran's IRGC said a second tanker carrying about 2 million barrels caught fire after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, after the first on Oct 17; IRNA said both had switched off positioning and radar and used a route Iran had not authorised. The ships' names were not released. CENTCOM disputes the mine claims: it says it has cleared the strait of mines and that vessels are being struck by projectiles, and it said the container ship GFS Pride, which sank on Oct 15, was hit by an IRGC projectile rather than a mine. UKMTO said at least 12 ships were attacked in the week to Oct 16, per Al Jazeera (AP, via CBS, reported 10), a weekly high since the war began on Feb 28, adding that most attacked vessels now refuse to report; one sank and two were disabled. AP reported that since early July most attacks have occurred off Oman, where the US military guides vessels. A tanker was hit by an RPG fired from a small boat about 78 nautical miles northeast of Jubail, and on Oct 18 a tug off the UAE was struck by two projectiles, with one minor casualty. CENTCOM's Adm. Brad Cooper said 400 ships and 100 million barrels moved through Hormuz in the past week; Kpler put flows at 11.6 million b/d in the seven days to Oct 13, about 68% of pre-war.

analysis.text: Most attacks are still off Oman, where US forces escort ships, but new strikes in the Gulf off Saudi Arabia and the UAE suggest Iran can reach shipping beyond the strait itself. Under-reporting by owners means the true risk is higher than official counts, which keeps insurance and freight costs climbing even when volumes hold.

causes.why: Second mine strike in two days in the same campaign

stories.unplaced: Speech at a military academy graduation; the outlets did not name the venue.
stories.title: Sisi says Egypt is ready to defend Saudi Arabia 'if requested'; Yemen rebuffs Iran's mediation
stories.summary: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said at a military academy graduation on Oct 17 that Egypt was ready to defend Saudi Arabia 'if requested', saying it was 'inconceivable' for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was harmed and that Egypt would 'carry out any measure to protect you or defend you'; he said any deployment needs parliamentary approval and 'we are speaking only about defense'. Yemen's foreign minister Afrah Alzouba rejected Iran's offer to mediate, made on Oct 16, saying Tehran 'has made itself a party to the war'. At an Organization of Islamic Cooperation meeting in Baghdad, Araghchi backed an 'inclusive' political process and met counterparts from Turkey, Egypt, Lebanon, Libya and Algeria. The Houthis released 159 pro-government fighters under an amnesty, the ICRC confirmed.

analysis.text: Egypt's stated aim is defense. The Yanbu-to-Suez route for rerouted Saudi crude has lifted canal revenue, but the war has also nearly tripled Egypt's monthly gas import bill, so Cairo is a net loser and is protecting what it can, along with its Saudi financial lifeline. A Cairo commitment would draw Egypt toward the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey Mecca pact, which it says it is seriously considering joining; Iran's mediation offer came a day before Sisi spoke and has been rebuffed.

sources.name: Türkiye Today (Egypt and the Mecca pact)

causes.why: Houthi fire on Saudi Red Sea exports threatens the route that feeds Suez
Riyadh's accusation framed Iran as a party, which Yemen's government echoed

stories.title: Missiles land at Aden airport; Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles aimed at Khamis Mushait
stories.summary: Two missiles landed on the grounds of Aden International Airport late on Oct 16, about 500 metres from a Yemenia flight preparing to leave for Cairo; Aden security blamed the Houthis, the second attack on the airport in under a week, and no casualties were reported. The Houthi-run Saba agency said the target was a military camp next to the airport. Early on Oct 18 the coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired toward Khamis Mushait and a drone aimed at Riyadh, where residents received a phone alert. Office tenants of Riyadh's Kingdom Center tower were told to work remotely. Houthi media said Saudi strikes killed 12 people in Taiz and Dhamar. The WSJ, citing people briefed on intelligence from Saudi Arabia and Yemen's anti-Houthi alliance, reported Iran is giving the Houthis targeting help, intelligence and training; Tehran denies a role. A Saudi National Guard helicopter crashed near Najran, killing two pilots; the coalition blamed a technical fault.

analysis.text: Striking Aden puts the government's seat and its Saudi backers' headquarters in range while Houthi forces hold the Bab el-Mandeb coast. The goal looks like pushing Riyadh toward a deal on Houthi terms rather than conquest of the south.

causes.why: Follow-on strike on Aden after the palace attack
Same Houthi missile campaign against the kingdom

stories.title: Russia fires 332 drones in 'one of its largest' strikes on Ukraine's grid
stories.summary: Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 332 attack drones, including 31 jet-powered ones, four Kalibr cruise missiles, Kh-22/32 cruise missiles and Iskander-M or KN-23 ballistic missiles overnight into Oct 17, and that 289 drones were downed; strikes hit 22 locations. Zelenskyy called it 'one of the largest strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure', saying more than 15 generation and transmission sites were targeted and Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Shepetivka, Slavuta and Netishyn were hit worst. Regional officials said seven people were killed and about 90 injured; FAB-250 glide bombs hit two apartment blocks in Sloviansk. The strike came the same night Trump signed his Oct 16 order waiving Graham Act sanctions; on Oct 16 Putin had ordered forces to continue 'massive and coordinated strikes'. Zelenskyy said the US decision to 'completely disregard' the Graham sanctions law 'only encourages' Putin. Ukraine's General Staff rejected Gen. Gerasimov's claim of 1,800 km² and 92 settlements taken since Sept 1; ISW assesses a net Russian loss of 122 km² in that period.

analysis.text: Western Ukraine's grid around the nuclear-linked Netishyn and Slavuta area is now a priority target, which stretches repair crews before winter. Inflated battlefield claims and grid strikes may be two halves of one message to Washington, that Russia is winning so Kyiv should be pressed; the strike was ordered before the waiver, so it was not a reply to it.

causes.why: Next night of the same pre-winter grid campaign
The strike coincided with the waiver the same night; at most the waiver removed a cost of pressing on

stories.unplaced: Reaction by lawmakers in statements and posts; no event site.
stories.title: Republicans and Democrats condemn Trump's Russia sanctions waiver, but Congress is in recess
stories.summary: Trump's Oct 16 executive order suspends sanctions and tariffs in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act until he or senior officials decide otherwise. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis called it 'beyond irresponsible', asking what part of 'enforcing a law passed 86-11' the administration did not understand; Sen. John Cornyn said the late Sen. Graham 'would be appalled'. Democrats Elizabeth Warren and Don Beyer accused Trump of enabling Putin. Congress is in recess until after the Nov 3 midterms. Rep. Gregory Meeks's bill to revoke the OFAC licences behind the US-Russia diesel deal has 16 Democratic co-sponsors and Republican Rep. Don Bacon.

analysis.text: The backlash is real but toothless before Nov 3: a veto-proof majority is unlikely, so the waiver will stand through the winter strike season. The likelier result is that Europe takes over more of the sanctions and financing burden.

causes.why: Direct reaction to the waiver

stories.title: Starlink ground-station arson in Poland traced to a Turkish gang allegedly hired by Russian intelligence
stories.summary: Der Spiegel reported, as relayed by Euronews on Oct 17, that the Sept 23 arson of a Starlink ground station at Wola Krobowska, south of Warsaw, leads to the Turkish organised-crime group 'Daltonlar', allegedly acting for Russian intelligence. The station helps route internet traffic including links used by Ukraine's armed forces. Two Turkish citizens were arrested in Nürtingen, Germany, on Oct 12 on Polish warrants for sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service; Poland's intelligence coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak said there was 'no doubt' Russian services were behind it. A fire also hit a Starlink site in Bulgaria on Oct 9. ISW said Polish authorities warn Russia may step up sabotage against logistics for Western aid this winter.

analysis.text: Using a professional crime syndicate rather than one-off recruits would mark an escalation in Russia's sabotage tradecraft, and the target choice links it to the fight over Ukraine's satellite communications at a time when Ukraine's Starshield service has been disrupted and the reasons are contested.

causes.why: Both bear on Ukraine's satellite communications, which Russia is targeting by sabotage

stories.title: France: 1,200 arrested as cost-of-living and school protests turn violent
stories.summary: About 550,000 people marched across France on Oct 17 against hardship in schools and the cost of living, and at least 1,200 were arrested, the BBC reported. Riot police used tear gas and water cannon in Paris; buildings were set alight, Limoges town hall's roof partly collapsed in a fire, and Lyon's historic tourist office burned. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 officers were injured and that some groups were using the protests as a 'warm-up' for the presidential election. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin asked prosecutors for an 'extremely firm' response; Macron said looters would be punished. Marine Le Pen accused Jean-Luc Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.

analysis.text: Energy-led inflation from the Hormuz shock is feeding the cost-of-living anger, and the April 2027 race between Le Pen and Mélenchon gives both flanks reason to keep the street hot. A weaker Paris means less European capacity to fill the gap the US leaves in Ukraine.

causes.why: Oil near $110 keeps European energy and food prices high

stories.title: Israeli drone strikes kill at least six in Gaza a year into the ceasefire; settlers attack diplomats
stories.summary: Israeli drone strikes on Oct 17 killed at least six Palestinians in Gaza City, near Jabalia, in Deir el-Balah and in Rafah's al-Mawasi area, medics said; Israel's army said it struck Hamas and Islamic Jihad operatives. Gaza's health ministry says 1,511 people have been killed since the Oct 10, 2025 ceasefire; UNICEF said more than 340 children have been killed since then. Al Jazeera mapping says Israel controls or restricts about 65% of the Strip. In the West Bank, settlers beat Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine and masked men reportedly attacked European diplomats near Taybeh; Netanyahu's office urged caution about the reports. Israel votes on Oct 27; polls are split: a Times of Israel poll has Gadi Eisenkot's party ahead with neither bloc at 61 seats, while Channel 14 polls have Likud ahead and the right-wing bloc at 61-62.

analysis.text: The 'ceasefire' has become a managed occupation with steady strikes, and settler violence is rising into the election. Attacks on EU diplomats raise the odds of European sanctions on settlers, while the outcome on Oct 27 will decide whether phase two of the Trump plan is revived or buried.

causes.why: Strikes continue because phase two never began

stories.unplaced: A statement about talks to be held in Tampa, Florida on Oct 20; the event has not happened yet.
stories.title: Lebanon's army delegation will demand an end to Israeli attacks at Oct 20 talks in Tampa
stories.summary: Lebanon's presidency said on Oct 17 that a military delegation will present Beirut's demand for an end to Israeli attacks at a trilateral meeting with Israel and the US in Tampa, Florida on Oct 20. Under a US-brokered deal Beirut pledged to disarm Hezbollah in return for a gradual Israeli withdrawal, but Hezbollah refuses to disarm while Israeli forces remain on Lebanese land, and Israel continues to strike southern Lebanon. The current war began on March 2.

analysis.text: Holding the talks at a US military hub signals Washington wants a security arrangement, not a political peace. Without a Hezbollah disarmament mechanism Israel is unlikely to give up its 'Yellow Line' positions before its Oct 27 election.

causes.why: Beirut's demands target the occupation zone Israel is hardening

stories.title: Pro-government forces claim Axum to Zalambessa; Rubio presses Abiy as Eritrea calls it 'war'
stories.summary: The Tigray Peace Forces said on Oct 17 that towns from Axum to Zalambessa are held by the Ethiopian army and the TPF, that most TPLF fighters have moved toward the Eritrean border and that disarmament is under way; witnesses reported fighting and Eritrean soldiers near the border. The Tigray Peace and Transformation Council said it was disbanding because the federal government will lead the transition directly. Ex-Tigray leader Getachew Reda told CGTN that Eritrea's Isaias Afwerki engineered the war and accused Egypt of arming Eritrea and Sudan of supplying drones to the TPLF; Eritrea's information minister called this false. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Abiy Ahmed to de-escalate. Ethiopia told the UN Security Council Eritrean troops had crossed its border; Eritrea called Ethiopia's moves a 'declaration of war'. A foreign security source told AFP 5,000-8,000 Eritrean soldiers are in Tigray.

analysis.text: With Tigray largely in federal hands, the live question is the Eritrea border, where Abiy's push for Red Sea access gives Addis a reason not to stop. The Egypt and Sudan allegations show the Horn war tying into Cairo's Nile dispute with Ethiopia and its new role backing Saudi Arabia across the Red Sea.

causes.why: Federal forces consolidate the sweep to the Eritrean border

stories.title: Army air strikes hit RSF seat in Nyala; RSF says 30 civilians died in a market
stories.summary: Sudan's army said Oct 16 air attacks on Nyala, capital of South Darfur and seat of the RSF's self-declared administration, killed dozens of RSF fighters and destroyed command centres. The RSF said an army drone hit a busy livestock market, killing 30 civilians including 17 women and five children; the rights group Emergency Lawyers said the drone was army-affiliated. Neither claim was independently verified. A government source told Al Jazeera the RSF hit mining sites in South Kordofan with drones. The Centre for Information Resilience reported army and allied Joint Forces gains in North Kordofan, including Sawdiri and al-Mazroub, while RSF drones keep hitting El Obeid, which shelters a growing displaced population.

analysis.text: Both sides are now fighting a drone war of attrition against each other's economic base, the RSF against gold mines and the army against the RSF capital, with civilians as the main casualties. The army's Kordofan gains make El Obeid the pivot of the war's middle front.

causes.why: Escalating drone exchange between the army and the RSF

stories.unplaced: Government decrees and statements; no event site.
stories.title: Kinshasa suspends Kabila's party and 12 others, grounds generals and freezes contacts with Belgium
stories.summary: DR Congo's interior minister ordered the suspension of 13 political parties, including Joseph Kabila's PPRD, in a decision dated Oct 15, days after Kabila launched the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) with M23. The defence ministry barred general and senior FARDC officers from leaving the country, and the presidency told staff to cut direct contact with Belgium's embassy after Belgian money-laundering raids on Oct 14, though no direct link has been officially established; the raids concern accusations against First Lady Denise Nyakeru Tshisekedi and family members, which she rejected. Belgian foreign minister Maxime Prévot called the ban unjustified. Government spokesman Patrick Muyaya told AFP that Kabila had 'decided to formalise his general attack' on the country.

analysis.text: Kinshasa is treating the FRN as an insurgency with a political wing, which narrows space for the opposition and for Qatar-led talks. Grounding the officer corps may mean Tshisekedi fears defections to Kabila as much as M23 on the battlefield.

causes.why: Crackdown responds to Kabila's FRN launch

stories.title: Pakistan and Afghan Taliban forces trade artillery fire for hours in Kurram
stories.summary: Pakistani state media said Afghan Taliban forces opened fire to 'facilitate terrorists' in the Taldah sector of Upper Kurram on Oct 17, and that the army answered with heavy weapons, destroying several posts and the Shipola base camp and reportedly killing several Taliban personnel. Afghan Taliban sources claimed seven Pakistani soldiers were killed in Paktia's Dand Patan district. Neither toll was verified. A day earlier Pakistan's foreign office said talks with Kabul 'could not be unconditional' and that it knew of no formal Russian mediation; Pakistan struck targets in Afghanistan on Sept 21 and Oct 1.

analysis.text: Islamabad is keeping military pressure on the Taliban while signalling it will take talks only on its terms, chiefly action against the TTP. The border war ties down troops Pakistan has pledged, in spirit, to its new Saudi and Turkish pact partners.

causes.why: Talks stalled, the border fighting resumed

stories.unplaced: KCNA did not say where the underwater test took place.
stories.title: North Korea says it tested an AI-guided 'super-speed' torpedo
stories.summary: KCNA said on Oct 17 that North Korea test-fired the Zam-2.0 super-speed precision-guided torpedo on Thursday, Oct 15, applying artificial intelligence to target detection and guidance, and called it 'a great success foreseeing a significant change' for the navy; it said more than 180 related tests had been run over five years. A day earlier Pyongyang fired two types of strategic cruise missiles from a presumed 3,000-ton submarine in the East Sea, and it recently commissioned the 5,000-ton destroyers Choe Hyon and Kang Kon. South Korea's military did not immediately comment.

analysis.text: North Korea is building a navy aimed at US carrier groups and South Korean ports, and the AI claim is partly propaganda. Russian technical help, repaid by North Korean missiles such as the KN-23 used on Ukraine, is a plausible accelerator.

causes.why: Continuing weapons-testing cycle

stories.title: Takaichi sends a Yasukuni offering as ministers visit; China 'strongly condemns'
stories.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sent a ritual offering to Yasukuni Shrine on Oct 17, and some cabinet members and lawmakers visited it. China's embassy in Japan 'strongly condemned' the moves, calling the shrine, which enshrines 14 Class-A war criminals, a 'symbol of Japanese militarism' and accusing Tokyo of paving the way for 'remilitarization'; it noted the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials.

analysis.text: An offering instead of a visit is Takaichi's usual calibration: it signals to her base without forcing a break. Beijing will add it to its case against Japan's defence build-up, which matters for rare-earth licensing to Japanese firms.

causes.why: Latest round in the China-Japan feud that began with Takaichi's Taiwan remarks

stories.title: Nine Chinese military and coast guard assets shadow a Philippine frigate at Scarborough Shoal
stories.summary: The Philippine Navy said Chinese PLAN warships 569 and 554, a supply ship, another warship, two China Coast Guard vessels, two drones and a maritime patrol aircraft shadowed the frigate BRP Miguel Malvar during a two-day patrol at Scarborough Shoal; Philippine air force, coast guard and fisheries patrols followed on Oct 16. China warned Manila against disrupting stability, and a Philippine lawmaker sought the expulsion of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan over the embassy's 'stop bluffing' taunt.

analysis.text: Beijing is matching each Philippine patrol with a larger mixed force, keeping the shoal under de facto Chinese control without firing. The envoy row suggests Manila's public diplomacy has hit a limit.

causes.why: Envoy row escalates as patrols continue

stories.unplaced: Activity spread across Taiwan's northern and central ADIZ; no single point.
stories.title: Taiwan tracks 2 PLA sorties, 5 navy ships and 9 'official' ships
stories.summary: Taiwan's defence ministry detected 2 PLA aircraft sorties, 5 PLAN ships and 9 official ships around Taiwan from 6 a.m. Oct 17 to 6 a.m. Oct 18 (UTC+8); both sorties crossed the median line into the northern and central ADIZ, and Taiwan responded with combat air patrols, navy ships and coastal missile systems.

analysis.text: The high count of government ships against few aircraft fits Beijing's shift toward coast-guard 'law enforcement' pressure seen at Dongsha this week.

causes.why: Continued coast-guard-heavy grey-zone pressure

stories.unplaced: A ministry notice opening public comment; no event site.
stories.title: China proposes export curbs on frontier AI models, chip designs and solar know-how
stories.summary: China's commerce and science ministries on Oct 16 proposed adding 40 technologies to the catalogue of prohibited and restricted exports: 23 in AI, 5 in biomedicine and 12 in solar, with 14 to be banned and 26 licensed. Core large-model technology, meaning weights, code and training methods, would be restricted at 10^26 operations of training compute, 2 trillion parameters or a global top-10 ranking; AI-processor designs are caught at 14 nm or finer among other triggers, and cluster know-how above 10,000 accelerators. API, app, SaaS and light on-device access are exempt, as are finished products and open-source work. Comment runs to Nov 15, and pre-export registration applies now.

analysis.text: Beijing is copying Washington's playbook, controlling the know-how rather than the service, so DeepSeek-style firms can still sell abroad while the state keeps a veto on transfers. Stacked on the Nov 10 rare-earth and battery deadline, it gives China more cards before any Trump-Xi bargain.

causes.why: Extends China's export-control leverage from minerals to AI know-how

stories.title: Plant fire pushes Cuba's forecast peak blackout to a record 75% as the peso hits 800 to the dollar
stories.summary: A fire on Oct 16 knocked out unit 1 of the Ernesto Guevara thermal plant at Santa Cruz del Norte, about 50 km from Havana, cutting available generation to 740 MW against peak demand of 2,900 MW; the grid operator projected a 2,190 MW shortfall, 75.5% of the island, the worst since statistics began in 2022, Infobae reported. Eight of the 16 thermal units were already out. Havana had 169 circuits dark on the morning of Oct 17. The shortfall eased on Oct 17, when the grid opened with 758 MW available and a 1,529 MW deficit. Cuba's energy crisis dates from mid-2024, with internal causes (an ageing grid with chronic underinvestment) and an island-wide blackout on Oct 18-22, 2024, and has been worsened since January by the US oil siege. The informal dollar rate hit a record 800 pesos (El Toque). Cuban state media reported drug shortages and blamed the US embargo ahead of the UN General Assembly vote on Oct 27-28; Cuba's UN envoy condemned a US 'Cuba Libre' event set for Oct 19.

analysis.text: Cuba's grid was already failing from age and underinvestment; the loss of Venezuelan oil and the US oil siege are pushing it down faster than solar can replace it. Washington is betting the crisis forces political change, but nearer risks are unrest and a new migration wave toward Florida.

causes.why: The US oil blockade starves the plants of fuel and parts

stories.title: Brazil's Oct 25 runoff is a dead heat between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro
stories.summary: A Vox Brasil poll taken Oct 15-17 gave Lula 51% of valid votes to Flávio Bolsonaro's 49%, within the margin of error. Datafolha (Oct 15) had Bolsonaro 51%, Lula 49% of valid votes (47% to 45% of total votes; Vox's total-vote figures were Lula 46.4%, Bolsonaro 44.6%), and Ipespe had Bolsonaro 48%, Lula 46%; PoderData/Aya found a 50-50 tie. Bolsonaro won the first round 47.03% to 45.16%. Lula said he backs lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 16 for heinous crimes, a shift toward the opposition's security line.

analysis.text: A Bolsonaro win would extend Latin America's right turn and align Brazil with Washington's hemisphere agenda; a narrow result either way raises the risk of a disputed count.

causes.why: Runoff race set by the first round

stories.title: Venezuela's US-backed talks turn to election rules; Machado's camp calls an Oct 22 march
stories.summary: The third round of US-sponsored talks opened in Caracas on Oct 14, hours after Washington lifted sanctions on government negotiator Jorge Rodríguez. Opposition delegate Dinorah Figuera said the agenda covers lifting candidate bans, restoring party symbols, renewing the electoral council and setting a vote date, with the bases ready before the end of 2026; Delcy Rodríguez says elections will happen but has named no date. María Corina Machado, left out of the talks, criticised the administration's oil deal with Alejandro Betancourt, and her platform called a nationwide mobilisation for Oct 22. OFAC issued General License 60A for earthquake relief on Oct 16.

analysis.text: Washington's priority is oil flow and stability under Delcy Rodríguez; a vote date is the price of legitimacy. Machado's exclusion splits the opposition and gives the government room to stall.

causes.why: Talks run alongside the US-managed reopening of Venezuelan oil

stories.title: Islamic State says it killed 400 JNIM fighters in Burkina's Oudalan; Bamako convoys keep fuel flowing
stories.summary: On Oct 12 Islamic State Sahel Province claimed it killed more than 400 JNIM fighters, including several leaders, in clashes days earlier (around Oct 8-9) in Burkina Faso's Oudalan province on the Mali and Niger borders; the toll is unverified, and ACLED's Heni Nsaibia said it would be the deadliest battle between the two if confirmed. UN experts call the rivalry 'the most intense direct confrontation globally' between al-Qaeda and IS affiliates, estimating JNIM at 7,000-8,000 fighters and IS at about 2,000. Separately, Malijet reported a convoy of 734 escorted fuel tankers reached Bamako on Oct 17, after 5,396 had arrived from September to Oct 10, despite JNIM's blockade.

analysis.text: The jihadist civil war bleeds JNIM, which may ease pressure on Bamako's fuel lifeline for a while, but it also spreads both groups into Niger and northwest Nigeria. Mali's convoys show it is managing the siege, not breaking it.

causes.why: JNIM is fighting the Malian state and IS at once after Kidal

relationships.stated: Egypt says it would defend Saudi Arabia 'if requested', and only in defense.
relationships.actual: Cairo depends on Saudi money and on Red Sea shipping; Saudi crude rerouted via Yanbu now props up Suez revenue, and both oppose Iran's reach and Ethiopia's Red Sea ambitions.
